newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish shares fall on Iraqi fighting.
newsitem.headline: Turkish shares fall on Iraqi fighting.

text.p: Turkish shares fell on Monday amid concern over neighbouring Iraq's attack in the Kurdish-held north and the possibility of Western intervention, brokers said.
"Today's uneasiness was due to the Iraqi fighting although all earlier (technical) indicators were in favour of the bourse," said Semih Cetin, general manager of Bayindir securities.
"There is anxiety because the fighting may spread and the U.S. may intervene," he added.

The Istanbul Stock Exchange index shed 1.95 percent to close at 63,275.86, although it rebounded slightly from a late low of 63,045. Of 217 shares traded, 171 declined while only 19 advanced and 27 were unchanged.
Daily trade volume shrank to 4.3 trillion lira ($49.3 million) from Thursday's 6.2 trillion ($72.3 million).
Iraqi troops captured the northern Iraqi administrative centre of Arbil on Saturday in a joint assault with the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), one of two leading Kurdish factions in the region.
Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said Baghdad's troops had left the city. But the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan faction said Iraqi soldiers remained and were carrying out mass executions.
Turkey said it will ask the United Nations and its Western allies to reverse a U.N. decision to delay a $2 billion oil-for-food plan for Iraq. Ankara hopes for a major stake in the resulting trade.
Bankers said Turkish money markets, dominated by a cash squeeze and focusing on a treasury-bill auction, shrugged off the Iraqi tension.
The Treasury will auction 112-day bills on Tuesday after sharply raising the average yield to 135 percent in last week's 189-day auction from 128.94 percent.

"Besides the developments in northern Iraq, the market is also worried about the Treasury's ability to borrow in domestic markets to meet its hefty T-bill repayments in September," said Cem Yalcinkaya from Garanti Investment Bank.
"The index will test support at around 63,000 amid the ongoing cash squeeze in the market. There is no fresh cash entry," Yalcinkaya said. $1=86760 lira
